newsitem.title: FIJI: Fiji says Australia must foster South Pacific ties.
newsitem.headline: Fiji says Australia must foster South Pacific ties.

text.p: Fiji Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka warned Australia on Tuesday that it could not ignore its island neighbours and must foster friendly relations in the wake of Australian documents critical of South Pacific nations.
"We are not in a canoe that we can row away in in this part of the world," Rabuka said before the start of a meeting with Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
"We are forever tied to the affairs of our neighbours and we will have to interact with each other," Rabuka said.

Downer's visit to Fiji is part of his first tour of the region since the embarrassing publication in July of Treasury department documents highly critical of the economies and leaders of many South Pacific nations.
The documents accused some ministers of corruption and said a number of the island nations' economies were on the verge of bankruptcy because of economic mismanagement.
South Pacific leaders at the time charged Australia with taking a "big brother" attitude towards its smaller neighbours, which are major recipients of Australian aid.
Downer said it was time the embarrassing documents were forgotten. "I think we all agreed that this is an incident that is best put behind us -- that's what we're all doing," he said.

Downer said the South Pacific was one of Canberra's main foreign policy priorities. "Together, we can build a better future for all of us," he said, adding the South Pacific would receive A$124.7 million (US$91.8 million) worth of Australian aid in the year to June 30, 1998.

Downer also said Australia would support Fiji's return to the Commonwealth of former British colonies following the introduction last month of a new constitution allowing for a multi-racial government.
Fiji was ejected from the Commonwealth in 1987 after declaring itself a republic following a military coup which overthrew a governmment then dominated by ethnic Indians.
It then passed a constitution in 1990 which guaranteed a parliamentary majority for ethnic Fijians.

Indians, who were brought to Fiji at the turn of the century to work on sugar plantations, now make up 45 percent of the country's 750,000-strong population and are influential in the business community.
